question: Studies suggest that children with physical disabilities report experiencing low self-efficacy when playing sport. Analyse how discrimination, stereotyping and prejudice can explain the children's low self-efficacy when applied to Bandura's model of self-efficacy.
markScheme:
Students are expected to answer in continuous prose, use good English, organise information clearly and use specialist vocabulary where appropriate.
AO1 - Knowledge of Bandura's model of self-efficacy, discrimination, stereotyping and prejudice.
Self-efficacy is affected by: performance accomplishments - how you have performed in a given situation previously; vicarious experience - seeing how people of a similar ability to you perform in a given situation; verbal persuasion - the verbal comments you receive from significant others regarding your ability to succeed; emotional arousal - whether your emotional arousal is at an optimal level or not.
Discrimination: unfair treatment of a person based on a stereotype or prejudice. Stereotyping: a preconceived idea about a group. Prejudice: a preconceived opinion that is not based on reason or actual experience.
AO2 - Application of Bandura's model of self-efficacy to children with a physical disability.
Performance accomplishments: children with a disability may have had a bad experience of playing sport in the past reducing self-efficacy/may have had limited or no opportunities to experience success.
Vicarious experience: children with a disability may have seen other children with a disability have a bad experience of playing sport, reducing self-efficacy/may have never seen another child with a disability having a positive experience.
Verbal persuasion: children with a disability may have heard significant others doubting their ability to succeed or been verbally dissuaded from taking part due to health and safety concerns.
Emotional arousal: children with a disability may feel more anxious playing sport due to increased risk/difficulty which may lead to over-arousal, decreasing self-efficacy.
Discrimination: if a performer with a disability is unable to access a club/team/sport without legitimate reason.
Stereotyping/prejudice: thinking that people with disabilities are not able to play sport/should only do certain activities.
AO3 - Analysis of how discrimination, stereotyping and prejudice would explain these feelings when applied to Bandura's model of self-efficacy.
Performance accomplishments: children with a disability may have encountered discrimination when playing sport, meaning they aren't given the opportunity to be successful, leading to a decrease in self-efficacy; this discrimination may be based on the stereotypical view that people with a disability can't play sport, or the prejudice that someone with a certain disability isn't as good as a performer without a disability.
Vicarious experience: discrimination by the media of sports played by people with a disability, based on the prejudice that it isn't as entertaining or exciting, may limit coverage; children with disabilities may not get the opportunity to see people with the same disability as them being successful in sport, meaning they begin to believe stereotypes, decreasing self-efficacy.
Verbal persuasion: people's stereotypical or prejudiced views that sport is dangerous/unsafe for people with disabilities may mean children hear a large number of negative, possibly discriminatory comments regarding their participation.
Emotional arousal: if children with disabilities encounter discrimination when participating in sport this may lead to anxiety, increasing arousal, leading to over-arousal which will decrease self-efficacy.
Accept any other appropriate analysis of how discrimination, stereotyping and prejudice can affect the children's low self-efficacy when applied to Bandura's model of self-efficacy.
Max 15 marks.

question: Despite the continued growth of women's rugby union, the number of qualified female rugby union officials remains relatively small and does not reflect the increase in the number of female players. Evaluate the effectiveness of the strategies being used to overcome specific barriers that may prevent women from becoming rugby union officials.
markScheme:
Students are expected to answer in continuous prose, use good English, organise information clearly and use specialist vocabulary where appropriate.
AO1 Knowledge of general barriers and strategies
Barriers (must be relevant to female officials): stereotypes/channelling; lack of media coverage; lack of role models; lack of sponsorship/full-time positions; lack of leisure time; fewer competitions.
Strategies: increased media coverage leading to more role models; more sponsorship/paid or full-time positions; education to overcome stereotypes; use of social media to create networks; laws and legislation to punish sexist behaviour/sex discrimination.
AO2 Application to female officials in rugby union
Barriers: there are currently a limited number of female officials (role models) and the majority work in the women's game, which is not covered extensively in the media; full-time refereeing positions in England are concentrated in the top tiers of men's rugby, with very few held by women; sexist abuse of the small number of female officials in the men's game may put other women off pursuing this route; there are fewer opportunities within the women's game due to the lower number of competitions.
Strategies: increased media coverage of women's rugby union would increase the profile of female officials in the sport; as the women's game becomes more professional, officials working in it should become professional too; punishing individuals who make sexist comments towards female officials would show that it will not be tolerated.
AO3 Evaluation of strategies which may overcome specific barriers
Increasing the media coverage of women's rugby union/female officials would increase the number of role models for other women to look up to; negative media coverage of female officials/sex discrimination may put women off; while social media can build support networks and provide information, there is an increased risk it may also be used to make sexist comments which will negatively impact the number of female officials; there is a lack of funding/sponsorship in the women's game, so the sport needs to prioritise where to spend it - is paying full-time officials the best use of this money, and would the pay be equal to the men's game; increased sponsorship of the women's game in recent years means there is more money in the sport, meaning officials who make good decisions are more important, so paying them as full-time will increase the standard and give more women something to aspire to.
Accept any other relevant evaluation of the effectiveness of the strategies being used to overcome specific barriers which may prevent women from becoming officials.
Max 8 marks.

question: Social stratification can impact on the sports participation of an individual. One example of social stratification is the social class that an individual belongs to. Evaluate the different sporting experiences that a 15-year-old from an affluent background and a 15-year-old from a low-income background may have, and how this might impact on their life-long participation in sport.
markScheme:
Students are expected to answer in continuous prose, use good English, organise information clearly and use specialist vocabulary where appropriate.
AO1 - Knowledge of social stratification and social class: social stratification is a type of social inequality where society is divided into different levels based on a social characteristic; social class is a term used to define social inequalities, eg certain groups have more access to wealth, income and power than others; factors which contribute to social class include a person's job, family background, education and income.
AO2 - Application of social class to experiences in sport (variety and amount): a 15-year-old from an affluent background is likely to have greater access to a wide range of sports, as they will be able to afford equipment, membership fees etc; they may also be better educated, having access to facilities at school and a greater understanding of the importance of being physically active; however, there may be greater pressure from parents/school for them to perform well academically, limiting time available for sport. A 15-year-old from a low-income background may not have access to as many sports as they may not be able to afford equipment/membership fees; their main provider of sporting experiences is likely to be their school; they may have less time to participate if they have a part-time job; it may be that they play more sport due to lower academic pressure, or see sport as a means of social mobility.
AO3 - Evaluation of impact on life-long participation: as the affluent 15-year-old is able to try more sports it increases the chances of them finding one they enjoy, and understanding the importance of physical activity means they are more likely to make time to take part; however they may be less likely to enjoy life-long participation due to job/career pressures or lack of motivation. The low-income 15-year-old may be limited in their likelihood of participating throughout life due to negative experiences, eg only playing sports they don't enjoy or using substandard facilities/equipment; alternatively they may be more likely to enjoy life-long participation due to sport providing income/escapism. Social class is not fixed and individuals may move between classes during their lifetime, impacting participation.
Credit other relevant evaluation of the different sporting experiences of a 15-year-old from an affluent background and a 15-year-old from a low-income background, and how this might impact on their life-long participation in sport.
Max 8 marks.

question: 'This Girl Can' is an example of a Sport England campaign that tries to increase female participation in sport by changing attitudes. Its adverts and posters typically show ordinary women of varying ages, shapes and abilities taking part in physical activity - for example running, cycling or lifting weights - looking energised, sweaty and confident, accompanied by slogans that challenge traditional expectations of how women should look and behave while exercising. Analyse how campaigns such as 'This Girl Can' might overcome barriers to female participation in sport and change attitudes.
markScheme:
Students are expected to answer in continuous prose, use good English, organise information clearly and use specialist vocabulary where appropriate.
AO1 - Knowledge of barriers to participation and attitudes: barriers to female participation may include lack of clubs, competitions, coaches, role models, media coverage, funding, accessibility; stereotyping/discrimination/low self-esteem/sexism. Three components of attitude: cognitive (how they think), affective (how they feel), behavioural (how they act). Attitudes can be changed by persuasive communication and cognitive dissonance.
AO2 - Application of barriers and attitudes to female participation in sport: traditional perception that some sports are for men and others for women (cognitive component); perception that some women may not like how it feels to play sport, being put off by being sweaty or getting muddy (affective component); women may avoid playing sport (behavioural component) because of how they believe others may perceive them; a female athlete may be channelled into typically feminine sports such as dance or gymnastics at school and not have the opportunity/access to sports such as rugby or boxing which, if given the chance, they may enjoy; 'This Girl Can' provides women with positive role models in its advertising, often accompanied by slogans which challenge traditional female stereotypes.
AO3 - Analysis of how campaigns can change attitudes: campaigns such as 'This Girl Can' change attitudes through persuasive communication and cognitive dissonance; persuasive communication is used by making role models out of ordinary women who enjoy being active, widely publicised alongside support from elite athletes; the message sent is that sport is not just for men, that you can take part and still be feminine, and that there is nothing wrong with getting hot and sweaty; as these adverts are widely seen they are likely to be viewed by women who want to make a change and may be inspired to take up a new activity; they also work via cognitive dissonance, changing one of the three components of an attitude to create an imbalance and increase the likelihood of change - the component impacted most is the cognitive component, how women and society think about women in sport; by showing women in sport in a positive light it may break down stereotypes and barriers leading to more women trying sport (behavioural component) and enjoying it (affective component); the campaign also raises the profile of women's sport which can result in more women-only sessions and clubs, increasing access and helping overcome barriers.
Credit other relevant analysis of how campaigns such as 'This Girl Can' might overcome barriers to female participation by changing attitudes.
Max 15 marks.

question: Aaron is a 20-year-old member of a local swimming club and has regularly competed in freestyle events since an early age. Evaluate the impact that socialisation could have had on Aaron's choices and his current involvement in sport.
markScheme:
Students are expected to answer in continuous prose, use good English, organise information clearly and use specialist vocabulary where appropriate.
AO1 - Knowledge of socialisation: socialisation is a lifelong process where members of a society learn its norms, values, ideas, practices and roles in order to take their place in that society. Socialisation has two phases: primary socialisation occurs during early years of childhood, usually within the immediate family; secondary socialisation occurs during later years (teenager to adult) when family are less involved and other agencies/people/groups have more influence. Gender socialisation is the act of learning to conform to gender roles through socialisation. Social control refers to the way in which people's thoughts, feelings, appearance and behaviour are regulated in social systems including social norms.
AO2 - Application of socialisation to Aaron as a male athlete: during primary socialisation, how active Aaron's parents and siblings were will have directly influenced his views on sport and physical activity; he will also have been influenced by the sports they played/watched/enjoyed. During secondary socialisation, his peer group and school will have had a greater influence on his choices.
AO3 - Analysis/evaluation of how socialisation will have impacted his choices: in the primary socialisation stage it is likely that Aaron developed an interest in swimming from his immediate family, who will also have been required to support him in his participation; had his family not had an interest in swimming it is unlikely he would have been involved from a young age. During secondary socialisation Aaron may have been further encouraged by his friends and teachers at school; had his friends/peer group not been supportive this may have resulted in Aaron giving up swimming or his involvement being reduced. Gender socialisation may have dictated the events within swimming that Aaron was drawn to, eg being drawn towards strength/power-based events typically associated with men.
Credit other relevant evaluation of the impact that socialisation will have had on Aaron's choices and development as an athlete.
Max 8 marks.

question:
The table below shows the participation data for disabled and non-disabled adults over a 4-year period since the London 2012 Paralympic Games:
% participating in 30 minutes of moderate intensity activity at least once per week (non-disabled) | % participating in 30 minutes of moderate intensity activity at least once per week (disabled)
2012-2013: 41.2 | 20.4
2013-2014: 40.9 | 18.7
2014-2015: 40.5 | 18.1
2015-2016: 40.8 | 17.5
Explain the barriers that disabled athletes face and evaluate the effectiveness of the strategies used to overcome these barriers. Use the data in the table above to support your answer.
markScheme:
Students are expected to answer in continuous prose, use good English, organise information clearly and use specialist vocabulary where appropriate.
AO1 - Knowledge of barriers and strategies for disabled athletes: barriers to participation include lack of facilities, funding, specialist coaches, specialist equipment, location, role models. Strategies to overcome barriers include increased media coverage, more role models, more funding.
AO2 - Application of barriers and strategies to participation for disabled athletes in the table: disabled participation may be lower due to low levels of media coverage; as there is a limited amount of disability sport on TV and in the news, disabled athletes may not be aware of the opportunities that exist or how to access them; increased media coverage is a strategy that can potentially help to overcome this barrier by increasing the number of role models. Participation rates for both groups, but especially for disabled athletes, are lower in 2015-16 than they were in 2012-13, suggesting a decline in participation following the London Games.
AO3 - Evaluation of effectiveness of strategies to overcome these barriers: increasing the media coverage of disabled sport would educate people on the capabilities of disabled performers, helping to overcome the myths and stereotypes that currently exist; however, TV stations rely on viewing numbers to gain income from sponsors and it is believed that disability sport would have a limited audience, so this may be unlikely to happen, and the figures from the table also imply that increased media coverage alone is not sufficient. Improving facilities and transport for disabled people would help them access the range of activities available; however, this would involve increased spending and investment, and sponsorship of disability sport is hard to come by due to limited exposure and low participation rates.
Credit other relevant analysis of the impact of prejudice, discrimination and stereotyping on disabled participation in sport, explaining the barriers they must overcome and suggesting possible solutions.
Max 15 marks.

question:
The table below shows the percentage of people in England taking part in physical activity at least once a week according to work status, over a five year period:
Work status | 2013/14 | 2014/15 | 2015/16 | 2016/17 | 2017/18
Full-time | 44.1% | 44.5% | 43.9% | 44.0% | 43.7%
Unemployed | 27.4% | 36.1% | 26.5% | 25.2% | 26.0%
Identify the barriers to participation for the disadvantaged and suggest possible solutions to overcome them. Refer to the table in your answer.
markScheme:
Possible content may include:
AO1 - Knowledge of barriers to participation: barriers include a lack of disposable income, lack of facilities, a lack of specialist equipment, location, emotional well-being.
AO2 - Application to the disadvantaged and reference to the table: the table shows that unemployed people participate in less physical activity than people in full-time employment in England, suggesting that socio-economic disadvantage is a barrier to participation; being unemployed means people won't have money to spend on gym membership or sports equipment, which can be expensive even for basics such as trainers. Some unemployed people may live in a poorer neighbourhood without many/any sports facilities, meaning they cannot afford to travel to an area with facilities. People who are unemployed may have low self-esteem and might not want to socialise with people through sport as a result.
AO3 - Possible solutions to overcome barriers to participation for the disadvantaged: leisure centres could offer discounted rates during the daytime for people who are unemployed or disadvantaged, and family discount rates to make participation more appealing and affordable; volunteers could be found to run free classes/coaching sessions for people who can't afford to pay, including youth clubs offering opportunities in deprived areas; clubs could offer sponsorship deals for talented performers from disadvantaged backgrounds so they can progress to elite level; local businesses could sponsor local clubs/schools in disadvantaged areas by providing kit/equipment, which is mutually beneficial. There was a boost in participation amongst the unemployed in 2014/15, which could have been linked to the London 2012 legacy still being felt, with unemployed people at home in the day watching more sport and being inspired by it. Government/sports organisations/local communities could introduce initiatives to promote the power of sport as a way to boost emotional well-being.
Accept any other relevant barrier to participation and solutions to overcome them. Answers must link specifically to the disadvantaged and the table to go beyond AO1.
Max 15 marks.

question: One objective of a recent Sport England strategy was to raise the percentage of females playing sport once a week. Data collected on once-a-week participation by gender shows consistently lower participation rates for females than males in netball, athletics and badminton, with athletics showing the smallest gap and netball the largest. Using this information, evaluate the sociological and psychological factors affecting female participation in netball, athletics and badminton.
markScheme:
Possible content may include:
AO1 - Knowledge of the sociological and psychological factors affecting female participation: sociological factors include discrimination, stereotyping, lack of access to clubs and competitive structures, limited curriculum time in schools, lack of media coverage, lack of sponsorship; psychological factors include social learning, reinforcement of feminine behaviour, formation and change of attitudes, and aggression.
AO2 - Application to female participation in netball, athletics and badminton: lack of interest in activities offered at school means fewer female students find an activity they enjoy enough to continue at club level; small number of lessons in the school PE curriculum for each activity means females do not have time to develop the skills and confidence to join local clubs; a narrower participation base means fewer numbers likely to progress to elite level; lack of media coverage means fewer role models to inspire the younger generation. Due to early socialisation, attitudes towards choice of activity are formed, eg perceiving netball or badminton as more 'suitable' than a contact-based activity.
AO3 - Evaluation of the sociological and psychological factors affecting female participation: netball has the largest participation gap, which could be attributed to fewer clubs/competitive structures for adult women outside school; athletics has the smallest gap, potentially due to strong female role models and wide media coverage during major championships; badminton's individual/social nature may make it more accessible, but still faces a gap linked to lack of club provision. Attitudes towards female participation would need to be changed through cognitive dissonance and challenging perceptions formed via social learning if participation gaps are to close; to maintain any change in attitude, there would need to be reinforcement of the new attitudes.
Credit other relevant evaluation of the sociological and psychological factors affecting female participation in netball, athletics and badminton.
Max 8 marks.
